7.Summary description of the proposed organizational change The College of Engineering proposes establishing a standalone Department of Biomedical Engineering Electrical,Computer,and Biomedical Engineering(ECBE).A standalone B ME department will elevate program visibility,strengthen student recruitment and enrollment,support faculty recruitment and retention,and promote stronger research collaborations and industry partnerships.
B.RATIONALE There should be a demonstrable purpose and documented need for the proposed organizational change. 1.
Explain why the organizational change is being proposed.
Biomedical engineering is a rapidly expanding interdisciplinary field bridging engineering, biology, and medicine.URl's B ME program has strong undergraduate enrollment,successful graduates,and faculty conducting nationally funded research in areassuch as wearable bio sensing,brain- machine interfaces,and neural robotics.Despite these successes,the program's administrative integration with EC BE limits its visibility,ability to tailor curricula,and competitiveness in recruiting faculty and students.

Establishing a standalone department will address these limitations, align with industry and workforce needs,and strengthen URl's role in biomedical research and education.
Theneed fora standalone Department of Biomedical Engineering at URl is reinforced by direct feedback from our key stakeholders and comparisons with peer institutions.Our graduates consistently emphasize the value of a clear,independent B ME identity,noting that it would strengthen their professional preparation,enhance visibility for research opportunities,and better position them inthe competitive job market.Similarly,members of research partners have recommended the establishment of an independent department as away to foster stronger industry and academic collaborations, attract high-caliber faculty, and provide a more focused administrative and organizational structure to support growth.

In addition,a review of peer and aspirational institutions shows that independent BME departments are the norm.Remaining administratively within EC BE places URl at a competitive disadvantage in student recruitment,faculty hiring,and research prominence.Creatinga standalone department addresses these gaps, aligning URl with national standards and ensuring the program can continue to thrive as a leader in biomedical engineering education and research.
C.INSTITUTIONAL ROLE The organizational change should be clearly related to the published role and mission of the institution and be compatible with the organizational structure of the institution. 1.Explain how the organizational change is consistent with the published role and mission of the institution and how it is related to institutional planning.
The creation of a standalone Department of Biomedical Engineering directly supports URl's mission to foster innovation, advance interdisciplinary research, and prepare graduates to meet the needs of aglobal society.It builds on existing strengths in engineering,health sciences,and statewide biomedical initiatives,aligning with institutional planning priorities and strategic goals.

2.Explain how the organizational change impacts other units and programs within the institution.
How have you communicated with the other units and programs about this proposed change, and what were the concerns raised relative to the organizational change?
The proposed organizational change to establish a standalone Department of Biomedical Engineering will have minimal impact on other units and programs within URl.The B ME program already exists aspart of Ec BE, and this transition does not reduce resources or capacity for other departments.Instead,it provides greater clarity in administrative structure and enhances opportunities for interdisciplinary collaboration acrossthe Collegeof Engineering and the broader university.

It will enhance interdisciplinary engagement through joint faculty appointments with units such as Kin es i ology,the Interdisciplinary Neuroscience Program(INP),and the Health Sciences,supporting shared teaching,co-advised students,and collaborative research across bio mechanics,neuroscience,rehabilitation,and translational health technologies.The department will also promote shared use of core facilities and research infrastructure,maximizing institutional resources and fostering cross-unit innovation.
Communication regarding the proposed organizational change has been ongoing and multi-level.
Discussions have taken place with faculty and leadership within ECBE,aswell as with other engineering departments,including Mechanical Engineering and Industrial Engineering.

Engagement has also occurred with the INP, Kin es i ology, and relevant health-related units through faculty meetings,individual consultations,advisory input,and regulars take holder updates.These conversations have helped shape the proposed structure and identify opportunities for collaboration and alignment.As a result of these discussions,wehave received support from ECBE,Kin es i ology,Mathematics and Mathematical Sciences,Interdisciplinary Neuroscience Program, and the Dean of the College of Engineering.
Overall,the proposed organizational change is designed to strengthen—not compete with—other expanding shared research opportunities,and creatinga transparent framework for resource planning.The establishment of a standalone B ME department is expected to enhance institutional cohesion and advance URl's broader goals in health,biomedical science, and interdisciplinary education.

D.INTER INSTITUTIONAL CONSIDERATIONS The organizational change should be consistent with all policies of the Boardof Trustees and the Rhode Island Department of Education pertaining to the coordination and collaboration between public institutions of higher education. 1.Estimate the projected impact of the organizational change on the other public higher education institutions in Rhode Island(e.g.,loss of students or revenues),provide a specific rationale of the assumptions made in the projections,and indicate the manner in which the other public institutions were consulted in developing the projections.Have you communicated with other institutions about the organizational change and have any concerns been raised related to role, scope,and mission or duplication?
The change is not expected to negatively impact other public higher education institutions in Rhode Island,as URl isthe only public institution in the state offering engineering degrees and has an established BME program.

Instead, the independent department will strengthen URl's competitive position regionally and nationally,potentially attracting students who might otherwise seek programs out of state.In developing the proposal,biomedical engineering departments and curricula at peer and aspirational universities were closely evaluated and discussed among BME faculty to ensure alignment with national norms and best practices.These evaluations informed

the proposed curriculum and departmental structure and reinforced that the change is consistent with the expected scope and mission of a standalone B ME department.
The primary assumption underlying the projected impact is that establishing an independent BME department will primarily retain and attract students who might otherwise pursue biomedical engineering programs outside of Rhode Island,rather than drawing students away from other in- state public institutions.
By improving program visibility, curricular alignment, and degree pathways,the proposed change is expected to strengthen URl's competitive position regionally and nationally.
Communication regarding the organizational change has occurred through internal institutional channels and faculty discussions,and no concerns have been raised related torole,scope,mission, or unnecessary duplication.

Given URl's unique role as Rhode Island's public engineering institution,the proposed change is expected to complement-rather than compete with-the broader public higher education ecosystem in the state. 2.List and describe any cooperative arrangements with other institutions relative to the organizational unit. On September 8, 2025, the Department of Electrical, Computer, and Biomedical Engineering (ECBE) convened a faculty meeting.
A total of 22 faculty members participated in the vote.
Of these, 20 were present in person, while two faculty members, who were unable to attend due to scheduling conflicts, cast their votes remotely during the meeting time.
In addition, you and Professor Emeritus Ramada Kumaresan attended the meeting as non-voting participants.

The faculty unanimously supported the following actions: (a) Initiating the process to seek approval for the Biomedical Engineering program to become the Department of Biomedical Engineering (BME). (b) Renaming the current ECBE department as the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering (ECE), contingent upon the establishment of BME as a separate department.
This decision was based on the vision for the future Biomedical Engineering department and the department-level resource allocation plan presented during the meeting.
Thank you for your continued leadership and support as we take this important step toward advancing the college's long-term vision.
This collective faculty decision reflects our readiness to support the next stages of the process under your guidance.

Williams May 7, 2026 Whereas, Travis Williams was elected Vice President and President-Elect of the Faculty Senate in spring 2024 and served as President from May 2025 to May 2026; and Whereas, he has served the University of Rhode Island Faculty Senate with distinction and dedication as Senate President; and Whereas, he has championed a collaborative approach to shared governance; and Whereas, he has brought a scripted – but not stilted – structure to the monthly meetings of the Faculty Senate; and Whereas, his written scripts for each meeting maintain order and are squirrelled away for use by future Officers; Whereas, he has prioritized outreach to deans and brought their voices and expertise into our discussions; and Whereas, his efforts to address concerns and build consensus before Faculty Senate meetings have facilitated the passage of important legislation; and Whereas, he has superbly navigated the Scylla and Charybdis of policy advocacy versus his role as neutral arbiter of Senate discussions and votes; and Whereas, he has kept an opinionated Executive Committee on task and been a truly superb mentor to his Vice President; and, finally, Whereas, he has often done all of this in less than two full hours; now Therefore, be it Resolved, that the University of Rhode Island Faculty Senate expresses its profound gratitude and congratulations to Travis Williams for his truly exceptional service and leadership as Senate President; and Be it further Resolved, that a copy of this resolution shall be presented to Travis Williams as a token of the Senate’s appreciation.

FOR CONFIRMATION BY THE FACULTY SENATE NEW PROGRAMS COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES BFA-Film, effective Fall 2026 Appendix A The Major.
The BFA in Film/Media is an intensive, experiential degree that integrates advanced creative practice with critical and historical study.
The curriculum emphasizes sequential training in film and media production alongside rigorous engagement with theory, research, and analysis.
Students develop technical and conceptual proficiency through sustained coursework, collaborative projects, and advanced culminating work that reflects professional standards and disciplined artistic inquiry.
FLM 496 (Capstone Seminar in Film/Media) and FLM 397 (1 Credit) BFA portfolio are required in the junior year; and FLM 497 (BFA Capstone) is required in the senior year.
Students learn to work with the evolving and overlapping technologies involved in the production of moving images.

A wide range of courses is available to the Film/Media student-courses that examine the historical, theoretical, and global approaches to the analysis and creation of moving images.
The Film/Media program prepares students for careers in such areas as independent filmmaking; animation and media design; film and television industries, advertising, marketing, public relations, and media criticism.
Graduates of this program are also prepared to continue with graduate studies in film and media production for an M.F.A.
Students majoring in the Film BFA must complete a minimum of 52 credits (maximum 67) in approved courses toward the major.
FLM 101 or FLM 101 H is a required prerequisite.
We recommend that students take at least one film production course per semester beginning with FLM 110 in their

freshman year, establishing a regular and consistent creative process.
The wide range of choices in Film/Media courses permits students to design a major that will meet both personal and professional goals.
Students must have a plan of study approved by an academic advisor in the Film/Media program before beginning their coursework in the major.
Degree Requirements: 120 total credits required for graduation, with minimum 30 credits numbered 300 or above.

COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES BA -Sustainable Food Systems, effective Fall 2026 Appendix B A BA in Sustainable Food Systems is ideal for students who wish to pursue a degree in food systems in the context of a liberal arts education.
Because the study and practice of food systems intersects with a wide range of other disciplines, the major is also ideal for those who wish to combine interdisciplinary training in food systems with a complementary major.
Students completing the program will graduate with the skills and knowledge needed to contribute to the development of sustainable, equitable, and resilient food systems from local to global scales.
The major allows participants to explore diverse aspects of the food supply chain from production to processing/distribution to consumption to waste management and recovery, with an emphasis on systems thinking, food system policy, and social, cultural, and political context.

By the time of degree completion, students will be uniquely positioned to enter the workforce in the growing field of sustainable food systems or to pursue opportunities in graduate education or research addressing the challenges of securing access to safe and affordable food for a growing population.
SFS BA students will pursue a curriculum offering breadth across the natural and social sciences and the arts and humanities.
The program entails a total of 120 credits, 30 credits of which must be in courses at the 300 level or above, including: A core sequence emphasizing an interdisciplinary and systems-approach to sustainable food systems.
Required courses include AFS/AVS/PLS 132G, an economics course (to choose from ECN 201, EEC 105, or INE 149), HSS/PSY 130G, NUT 207, one course in sustainability (3 credits minimum, to choose from SUS 102, SAF 305, COM/SUS 108G, COM/SUS 315, COM/SUS 460, and other relevant courses), APG/GWS/SOC 308, SAF 383, and one course in sustainable production (3 credits minimum, to choose from AFS 105G/106, AVS 101/102, or PLS 150).
A minimum of two electives related to food systems at the 300 level or above (6 credits minimum).

A robust capstone experience in which students master the ability to address the complex challenges in the area of sustainable food systems through experiential learning in interdisciplinary teams.
Students are required to take a total of six credits, including three credits of internship or special project and an additional three credits in another capstone course.
Current examples of capstone courses include AFS 440, PLS 385, and SAF 400G.
Compared to the BS in SFS, the BA allows students greater flexibility in selecting courses relevant to their specific interests.
In addition, students may have more flexibility in combining this major with a complementary major in another subject to gain greater breadth of experience they can apply to their future careers.
